claim: Cortical networks exhibit 'global oscillations', in which neural spike times are entrained to an underlying oscillatory rhythm.
source: Cortical networks exhibit 'global oscillations', in which neural spike times are entrained to an underlying oscillatory rhythm, but where individual neurons fire irregularly, on only a fraction of cycles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of cortical network behavior.

claim: In global oscillations, individual neurons fire irregularly, on only a fraction of cycles.
source: Cortical networks exhibit 'global oscillations', in which neural spike times are entrained to an underlying oscillatory rhythm, but where individual neurons fire irregularly, on only a fraction of cycles.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a characterization of cortical network behavior.

claim: Global oscillations are a direct consequence of optimal efficient coding in spiking networks with synaptic delays and noise.
source: Here, we show that such global oscillations are a direct consequence of optimal efficient coding in spiking networks with synaptic delays and noise.
evidence: This is the main claim of the paper, supported by computational modeling and simulations throughout the manuscript.

claim: To avoid firing unnecessary spikes, neurons need to share information about the network state.
source: To avoid firing unnecessary spikes, neurons need to share information about the network state.
evidence: This is stated as a principle underlying efficient coding in the abstract.

claim: Ideally, membrane potentials should be strongly correlated and reflect a 'prediction error' while the spikes themselves are uncorrelated and occur rarely.
source: Ideally, membrane potentials should be strongly correlated and reflect a 'prediction error' while the spikes themselves are uncorrelated and occur rarely.
evidence: This is stated as an ideal condition for efficient coding in the abstract.

claim: The most efficient representation is when spike times are entrained to a global Gamma rhythm.
source: We show that the most efficient representation is when: (i) spike times are entrained to a global Gamma rhythm (implying a consistent representation of the error); but (ii) few neurons fire on each cycle (implying high efficiency), while (iii) excitation and inhibition are tightly balanced.
evidence: This is one of the main findings stated in the abstract and supported by simulations.

claim: The most efficient representation is when few neurons fire on each cycle.
source: We show that the most efficient representation is when: (i) spike times are entrained to a global Gamma rhythm (implying a consistent representation of the error); but (ii) few neurons fire on each cycle (implying high efficiency), while (iii) excitation and inhibition are tightly balanced.
evidence: This is one of the main findings stated in the abstract and supported by simulations.

claim: The most efficient representation is when excitation and inhibition are tightly balanced.
source: We show that the most efficient representation is when: (i) spike times are entrained to a global Gamma rhythm (implying a consistent representation of the error); but (ii) few neurons fire on each cycle (implying high efficiency), while (iii) excitation and inhibition are tightly balanced.
evidence: This is one of the main findings stated in the abstract and supported by simulations.

claim: Cortical networks exhibiting global oscillations, sparse firing, and tight excitation-inhibition balance are tuned to achieve a maximally efficient population code.
source: This suggests that cortical networks exhibiting such dynamics are tuned to achieve a maximally efficient population code.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, based on the modeling results.

claim: In sensory areas, one typically observes 'global oscillations' in the gamma-band range (30–80 Hz).
source: In sensory areas, one typically observes 'global oscillations' in the gamma-band range (30–80 Hz), alongside single neuron responses that are irregular and sparse (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Yu and Ferster, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with supporting citations.

claim: Single neuron responses in sensory areas are irregular and sparse.
source: In sensory areas, one typically observes 'global oscillations' in the gamma-band range (30–80 Hz), alongside single neuron responses that are irregular and sparse (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Yu and Ferster, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with supporting citations.

claim: The magnitude and frequency of gamma-band oscillations are modulated by changes to the sensory environment.
source: The magnitude and frequency of gamma-band oscillations are modulated by changes to the sensory environment (e.g. visual stimulus contrast (Henrie and Shapley, 2005) and behavioural state (e.g. attention [Fries et al., 2001]) of the animal.
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with supporting citations.

claim: Visual stimulus contrast modulates the magnitude and frequency of gamma-band oscillations.
source: The magnitude and frequency of gamma-band oscillations are modulated by changes to the sensory environment (e.g. visual stimulus contrast (Henrie and Shapley, 2005) and behavioural state (e.g. attention [Fries et al., 2001]) of the animal.
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with a supporting citation.

claim: Attention modulates the magnitude and frequency of gamma-band oscillations.
source: The magnitude and frequency of gamma-band oscillations are modulated by changes to the sensory environment (e.g. visual stimulus contrast (Henrie and Shapley, 2005) and behavioural state (e.g. attention [Fries et al., 2001]) of the animal.
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with a supporting citation.

claim: Neural oscillations play a fundamental role in cortical computation.
source: This has led a number of authors to propose that neural oscillations play a fundamental role in cortical computation (Fries, 2009; Engel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis proposed by other researchers, with supporting citations.

claim: Oscillations emerge as a consequence of interactions between populations of inhibitory and excitatory neurons, and do not perform a direct functional role in themselves.
source: Others argue that oscillations emerge as a consequence of interactions between populations of inhibitory and excitatory neurons, and do not perform a direct functional role in themselves (Ray and Maunsell, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an alternative hypothesis proposed by other researchers, with a supporting citation.

claim: The 'efficient coding hypothesis' posits that the role of early sensory processing is to communicate information about the environment using a minimal number of spikes.
source: A prevalent theory of sensory processing, the 'efficient coding hypothesis', posits that the role of early sensory processing is to communicate information about the environment using a minimal number of spikes (Barlow, 1961).
evidence: This is stated as an established theory with a supporting citation.

claim: According to efficient coding, the responses of individual neurons should be as asynchronous as possible, so that they do not communicate redundant information.
source: This implies that the responses of individual neurons should be as asynchronous as possible, so that they do not communicate redundant information (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the efficient coding hypothesis with a supporting citation.

claim: Oscillations are generally seen as a bad thing for efficient rate coding, as they tend to synchronise neural responses, and thus, introduce redundancy.
source: Thus, oscillations are generally seen as a bad thing for efficient rate coding, as they tend to synchronise neural responses, and thus, introduce redundancy.
evidence: This is stated as a common view in the field.

claim: Greatest accuracy in encoding a constant sensory variable is achieved when the population fires at regular intervals, but no two neurons fire together.
source: Greatest accuracy is achieved when the population fires at regular intervals, but no two neurons fire together (left).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1a and illustrated in the figure.

claim: Coding accuracy is reduced when multiple neurons fire together.
source: Coding accuracy is reduced when multiple neurons fire together (middle and right panels).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1a and illustrated in the figure.

claim: Reconstruction error increases with the number of synchronous spikes per cycle in a regular spiking network.
source: Figure 1c shows how, in the regular spiking network described above, coding error increases with the number of synchronous spikes per cycle (while firing rate is held constant).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1c.

claim: A completely asynchronous network, in which neurons fire with independent Poisson variability, performs far worse than the regular spiking network, even when multiple neurons fire together on each cycle.
source: However, one also observes that a completely asynchronous network, in which neurons fire with independent Poisson variability (Figure 1b), performs far worse than the regular spiking network, even when multiple neurons fire together on each cycle (Figure 1c, horizontal dashed line).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 1b and 1c.

claim: To perform efficiently, neural networks face a trade-off between coordinating activity for an efficient code and avoiding over-synchronization due to synaptic delays.
source: Thus, to perform efficiently, neural networks face a trade-off (Figure 1d). On the one hand, recurrent connections should coordinate the activity of different neurons in the network, so as to achieve an efficient and accurate population code. On the other hand, in the presence of synaptic delays, it is important that these recurrent signals do not overly synchronize the network, as this will reduce coding performance.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1d.

claim: Inhibitory connections are subject to unavoidable delays (e.g. synaptic and transmission delays).
source: To achieve this ideal, however, requires incredibly fast inhibitory connections, so that each time a neuron fires a spike it suppresses all other neurons from firing (Boerlin et al., 2013). In reality, inhibitory connections are subject to unavoidable delays (e.g. synaptic and transmission delays), and thus, cannot always prevent neurons from firing together.
evidence: This is stated as a biological constraint.

claim: In the presence of delays, inhibitory signals intended to prevent neurons from firing together can actually synchronise the network.
source: Worse, in the presence of delays, inhibitory signals, intended to prevent neurons from firing together, can actually have the reverse effect of synchronising the network, so that many neurons fire together on each cycle (as in Figure 1a, middle and right panels).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claim: The synchronization effect due to delays is analogous to the 'hipster effect' where delayed reaction times lead to similar decisions.
source: This is analogous to the so-called 'hipster effect' where a group of individuals strive to look different from each other, but due to delayed reaction times, end up making similar decisions and all looking alike (Touboul and Effect, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as an analogy with a supporting citation.

claim: In a network of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons optimized for efficient coding, the trade-off is best met by adding noise to ensure spike trains are entrained to a global oscillatory rhythm but only a small fraction of cells fire on each oscillation cycle.
source: Here, we show that, in a network of leaky integrate-and-fire neurons (LIF) optimized for efficient coding, this trade-off is best met by adding noise to the network (e.g. via random fluctuations in membrane potential, or synaptic failure) to ensure that: (i) neural spike trains are entrained to a global oscillatory rhythm (for a consistent representation of global information), but (ii) only a small fraction of cells fire on each oscillation cycle.
evidence: This is one of the main findings of the paper, supported by simulations.

claim: In the optimal regime, individual neurons fire irregularly.
source: In this regime, individual neurons fire irregularly (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998) and exhibit weak pairwise correlations (Schneidman et al., 2006), despite the presence of rhythmic population activity.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the optimal regime with supporting citations.

claim: In the optimal regime, neurons exhibit weak pairwise correlations, despite the presence of rhythmic population activity.
source: In this regime, individual neurons fire irregularly (Shadlen and Newsome, 1998) and exhibit weak pairwise correlations (Schneidman et al., 2006), despite the presence of rhythmic population activity.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the optimal regime with supporting citations.

claim: In the optimal regime, excitation and inhibition are tightly balanced on each oscillation cycle, with inhibition lagging excitation by a few milliseconds.
source: Moreover, excitation and inhibition are tightly balanced on each oscillation cycle, with inhibition lagging excitation by a few milliseconds (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Wehr and Zador, 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the optimal regime with supporting citations.

claim: When a neuron's membrane potential becomes larger than a constant threshold, then it fires a spike.
source: When a neuron's membrane potential becomes larger than a constant threshold, then it fires a spike; recurrent feedback then reduces the prediction error encoded by other neurons, preventing them from firing further redundant spikes.
evidence: This is stated as a principle of the model.

claim: Recurrent feedback reduces the prediction error encoded by other neurons, preventing them from firing further redundant spikes.
source: When a neuron's membrane potential becomes larger than a constant threshold, then it fires a spike; recurrent feedback then reduces the prediction error encoded by other neurons, preventing them from firing further redundant spikes.
evidence: This is stated as a principle of the model.

claim: Each time a neuron fires a spike, it increases the reconstruction by a fixed amount, decreasing the difference between the input and the neural reconstruction.
source: Each time a neuron fires a spike, it increases the reconstruction by a fixed amount, decreasing the difference between the input and the neural reconstruction.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Immediately after a spike, feedback connections alter the membrane potentials of other neurons, to ensure that they maintain a consistent representation of the error, and do not fire further spikes.
source: Immediately after, feedback connections alter the membrane potentials of other neurons, to ensure that they maintain a consistent representation of the error, and do not fire further spikes (Figure 2b, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model shown in Figure 2b.

claim: In the idealized efficient coding network, membrane potentials are highly correlated, while spikes are asynchronous.
source: As a result, membrane potentials are highly correlated, while spikes are asynchronous.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the idealized model.

claim: To optimally encode a constant input, the network generates a regular train of spikes.
source: To optimally encode a constant input, the network generates a regular train of spikes (as in the left panel of Figure 1a), resulting in a narrow distribution of population inter-spike intervals (ISIs) (Figure 2d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2c and 2d.

claim: Neural membrane potentials, which encode a common prediction error, fluctuate in synchrony, with a frequency dictated by the population firing rate.
source: Neural membrane potentials, which encode a common prediction error, fluctuate in synchrony, with a frequency dictated by the population firing rate (Figure 2c, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2c.

claim: As only one neuron fires per cycle in the idealized network, the spike trains of individual neurons are irregular and sparse, resulting in a near-exponential distribution of single-cell ISIs.
source: However, as only one neuron fires per cycle, the spike trains of individual neurons are irregular and sparse, resulting in a near-exponential distribution of single-cell ISIs (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Even very short synaptic delays can profoundly change the behaviour of the idealized efficient coding network, and pose fundamental limits on its performance.
source: Far from being a biological detail, even very short synaptic delays can profoundly change the behaviour of the idealized efficient coding network, and pose fundamental limits on its performance.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding about the effect of synaptic delays.

claim: Inhibitory neurons fire spikes in order to predict and cancel the inputs to the excitatory population.
source: Inhibitory neurons, which receive input from excitatory neurons, fire spikes in order to predict and cancel the inputs to the excitatory population.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the model with separate excitatory and inhibitory populations.

claim: The inhibitory reconstruction closely tracks fluctuations in the excitatory reconstruction.
source: Consequently, the inhibitory reconstruction closely tracks fluctuations in the excitatory reconstruction (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the model design.

claim: Without delays, recurrent inhibition prevents all but one cell from firing per oscillation cycle, resulting in an optimally efficient code.
source: Without delays, recurrent inhibition prevents all but one cell from firing per oscillation cycle, resulting in an optimally efficient code (Figure 3c, left panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3c.

claim: With delays, inhibition cannot always act fast enough to prevent neurons firing together, and neural activity quickly becomes synchronised.
source: With delays however, inhibition cannot always act fast enough to prevent neurons firing together. As a result, neural activity quickly becomes synchronised, and the sensory reconstruction is destroyed by large population-wide oscillations (Figure 3c, middle panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3c.

claim: Increasing the membrane potential noise and spike threshold can reduce the chance of neurons firing together and improve performance in the presence of delays.
source: To improve performance, one can increase the membrane potential noise and spike threshold, so as to reduce the chance of neurons firing together (Figure 3c, right panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 3c.

claim: Too much noise causes the firing of different neurons to become uncoordinated, diminishing network performance.
source: Too much noise, however, and the firing of different neurons becomes uncoordinated, and network performance is diminished (see later).
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of excessive noise.

claim: In the Poisson network, random fluctuations in firing rate degrade the reconstruction, resulting in large coding error.
source: In the Poisson network, random fluctuations in firing rate degrade the reconstruction, resulting in large coding error.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the Poisson network comparison.

claim: Increasing the population firing rate in the Poisson network increases the signal-to-noise ratio, and thus, also decreases the reconstruction error.
source: Increasing the population firing rate increases the signal-to-noise ratio, and thus, also decreases the reconstruction error (Figure 3d, red).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: In the 'ideal' efficient coding network, noise fluctuations are automatically corrected for by the recurrent connections.
source: In contrast, in the 'ideal' efficient coding network, noise fluctuations are automatically corrected for by the recurrent connections (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the ideal efficient coding network.

claim: In the ideal efficient coding network, the only source of inaccuracy comes from the discreteness of the code, leading to a small error.
source: Thus, in this network, the only source of inaccuracy comes from the discreteness of the code (where each spike adds a fixed quantity to the readout), leading to a small error (Figure 3d, blue).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: While synaptic delays increase the coding error relative to the ideal efficient coding network, the error remains significantly smaller than for a Poisson network with the matching rate.
source: Finally, while synaptic delays increase the coding error (relative to the ideal efficient coding network), the error remains significantly smaller than for a Poisson network with the matching rate (Figure 3d, black cross).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3d.

claim: With synaptic delays, several neurons fire together before the arrival of recurrent inhibition.
source: However, with synaptic delays, several neurons fire together before the arrival of recurrent inhibition.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model with delays.

claim: With synaptic delays, oscillations are slower and larger in magnitude than for the idealised network, where only one neuron fires on each cycle.
source: As a result, oscillations are slower and larger in magnitude than for the idealised network, where only one neuron fires on each cycle.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between the network with and without delays.

claim: Increasing the magnitude of the membrane potential noise desynchronized the network activity, resulting in a reduction in pairwise voltage correlations.
source: Increasing the magnitude of the membrane potential noise desynchronized the network activity, resulting in a reduction in pairwise voltage correlations (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4a.

claim: With increased noise, single neural spike trains became more irregular, reflected by an increase in the spiking CV.
source: With increased noise, single neural spike trains also became more irregular, reflected by an increase in the spiking CV (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Coding performance varied non-monotonically with the noise amplitude, following a u-shaped curve.
source: Coding performance, however, varied non-monotonically with the noise amplitude. The reconstruction error followed a u-shaped curve, being minimised for a certain intermediate level of noise (Figure 4c, solid curve).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: For the intermediate noise level, coding performance was significantly better than a network of independent Poisson units with a matching firing rate.
source: For this intermediate noise level, coding performance was significantly better than a network of independent Poisson units with a matching firing rate (horizontal dashed line).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Deviations between excitation and inhibition followed a u-shape curve, being minimised for the same intermediate noise level as optimal coding.
source: Interestingly, deviations between excitation and inhibition followed a similar u-shape curve, being minimised for the same intermediate noise level (Figure 4c, thick dashed curve).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Optimal coding was achieved when the balance between excitatory and inhibition was the tightest.
source: Thus, optimal coding was achieved when the balance between excitatory and inhibition was the tightest.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results shown in Figure 4c.

claim: At the optimal level of noise, the spiking CV value was near unity, implying irregular (near-poisson) single cell responses.
source: Further, at the optimal level of noise, the spiking CV value was near unity (Figure 4b), implying irregular (near-poisson) single cell responses.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4b.

claim: With low noise, neural membrane potentials were highly correlated, leading many neurons to fire together on each oscillation cycle.
source: With low noise, neural membrane potentials were highly correlated, leading many neurons to fire together on each oscillation cycle (Figure 4d, upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: With low noise, the neural reconstruction exhibited large periodic fluctuations about the encoded input, leading to poor coding performance.
source: As a result, the neural reconstruction exhibited large periodic fluctuations about the encoded input, leading to poor coding performance (Figure 4d, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4d.

claim: When the injected noise was very high, the spike trains of different neurons were uncorrelated.
source: At the other extreme, when the injected noise was very high, the spike trains of different neurons were uncorrelated (Figure 4f, upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In the high noise regime, effectively no information was shared between neurons, inhibitory and excitatory reconstructions were decoupled, and coding performance was similar to a population of independent Poisson units.
source: As, in this regime, effectively no information was shared between neurons, inhibitory and excitatory reconstructions were decoupled, and coding performance was similar to a population of independent Poisson units (Figure 4f, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4f.

claim: In the intermediate noise regime, for which performance was optimal, spikes were aligned to rhythmic fluctuations in the prediction error, but few neurons fired on each cycle.
source: In the intermediate noise regime, for which performance was optimal, spikes were aligned to rhythmic fluctuations in the prediction error, but few neurons fired on each cycle (Figure 4e, upper panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4e.

claim: In the intermediate noise regime, the network exhibited a near-exponential distribution of interspike-intervals, coupled with a narrow peak in the population firing rate spectrum.
source: These dynamics were reflected by a near-exponential distribution of interspike-intervals (Figure 4e), coupled with a narrow peak in the population firing rate spectrum (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4g and 4h.

claim: In the intermediate noise regime, rhythmic fluctuations in the neural reconstruction were small in magnitude, and there was a tight coupling between inhibitory and excitatory reconstructions.
source: In this regime, rhythmic fluctuations in the neural reconstruction were small in magnitude, and there was a tight coupling between inhibitory and excitatory reconstructions (Figure 4e, lower panel).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Qualitatively similar changes in coding performance and network synchrony were observed regardless of how noise was manipulated in the network (membrane potential noise, synaptic failures, or random Poisson firing).
source: We observed qualitatively similar changes in coding performance and network synchrony, regardless of how we manipulate noise in the network.
evidence: This is stated as a general finding after manipulating noise in different ways.

claim: In both synaptic failure and random Poisson firing manipulations, the coding error was smaller at an intermediate level of noise, for which there was tightest balance between inhibition and excitation.
source: In both cases, the coding error was smaller at an intermediate level of noise, for which there was tightest balance between inhibition and excitation (Figure 5a and c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a and 5c.

claim: The population firing rate was characterised by a transient peak following stimulus onset, followed by decay to a constant value.
source: The population firing rate was characterised by a transient peak following stimulus onset, followed by decay to a constant value.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the model shown in Figure 6a.

claim: A spectrogram of the population firing rate reveals the presence of 30–50 Hz oscillations during the period of sustained activity.
source: A spectrogram of the population firing rate (Figure 6a, lower panel) reveals the presence of 30–50 Hz oscillations during the period of sustained activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Correlated rhythmic fluctuations in excitatory and inhibitory activity are observed during sustained activity.
source: Here, one clearly sees correlated rhythmic fluctuations in excitatory (black) and inhibitory (red) activity.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from Figure 6b.

claim: The strength of oscillations increases with stimulus amplitude.
source: The strength of these oscillations increases with stimulus amplitude (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: For all input amplitudes, individual neurons fired irregularly, with a near-exponential distribution of inter-spike intervals.
source: Nevertheless, for all input amplitudes, individual neurons fired irregularly, with a near-exponential distribution of inter-spike intervals (Figure 6d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6d.

claim: In area V1, visual stimulation increases gamma-band correlations between pairs of neural membrane potentials.
source: Previously, Yu & Ferster (Yu and Ferster, 2010) reported that, in area V1, visual stimulation increases gamma-band correlations between pairs of neural membrane potentials (Figure 7a).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation from a cited study, with data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: The model produces qualitatively similar results to Yu & Ferster's observations, with increased correlations between neural membrane potentials when feed-forward input amplitude is increased.
source: Qualitatively similar results were obtained with our model (Figure 7b). Increasing the amplitude of the feed-forward input led to increased correlations between neural membrane potentials (Figure 7c), with strongest coherence observed in the gamma-band range (Figure 7d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 7b, 7c, and 7d.

claim: Increasing the amplitude of the feed-forward input leads to more neurons firing spikes on each cycle, leading to stronger oscillations.
source: This is because more neurons fire spikes on each cycle, leading to stronger oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for the increased correlations with increased input.

claim: Several studies have reported a tight balance between inhibition and excitation.
source: Several studies have reported a tight balance between inhibition and excitation (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Cafaro and Rieke, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with supporting citations.

claim: Atallah et al. reported that inhibitory and excitatory currents are precisely balanced on individual cycles of an ongoing gamma oscillation.
source: Recently, Atallah et al. (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009) reported that inhibitory and excitatory currents are precisely balanced on individual cycles of an ongoing gamma oscillation (Figure 8a).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation from a cited study, with data shown in Figure 8a.

claim: In the model, efficient coding is achieved by maintaining a tight balance between inhibitory and excitatory reconstructions.
source: In our model, efficient coding is achieved by maintaining such a tight balance between inhibitory and excitatory reconstructions.
evidence: This is stated as a principle of the model.

claim: In the model, inhibitory and excitatory currents closely track each other, with a high correlation between the amplitude of inhibitory and excitatory currents on each cycle.
source: Thus, inhibitory and excitatory currents closely track each other (Figure 8b), with a high correlation between the amplitude of inhibitory and excitatory currents on each cycle (Figure 8c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 8b and 8c.

claim: In common with Atallah et al.'s data, inhibition lags behind excitation by a few milliseconds in the model.
source: In common with Atallah et al.'s data, inhibition lags behind excitation by a few milliseconds (Figure 8d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8d.

claim: Fluctuations in the amplitude of inhibitory and excitatory currents instantaneously modulate the oscillation frequency, with a significant correlation observed between the peak amplitude on a given oscillation cycle and the period of the following cycle.
source: Fluctuations in the amplitude of inhibitory and excitatory currents instantaneously modulate the oscillation frequency, with a significant correlation observed between the peak amplitude on a given oscillation cycle and the period of the following cycle (Figure 8e).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8e.

claim: The optimal network parameters depend on the properties of the feed-forward sensory input.
source: In general, the optimal network parameters depend on the properties of the feed-forward sensory input.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle.

claim: The higher the input amplitude, the more noise is required to achieve the optimal level of network synchrony.
source: For example, the higher the input amplitude, the more noise is required to achieve the optimal level of network synchrony (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 9a.

claim: While the network achieves reasonable coding accuracy for a large range of different inputs, adaptive tuning of the dynamics can be beneficial for a more limited input range.
source: While the network achieves reasonable coding accuracy for a large range of different inputs, adaptive tuning of the dynamics (for example, changing the noise level) can be beneficial for a more limited input range.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about network performance.

claim: Adaptive tuning of network dynamics would affect the level of population synchrony and thus introduce a correlation between performance and the strength of Gamma oscillations.
source: This would affect the level of population synchrony and thus introduce a correlation between performance and the strength of Gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of adaptive tuning.

claim: If the task is to detect weak (low amplitude) inputs, performance would be higher if top down modulations (such as attention) reduced the level of noise, and thus increased the degree of population synchrony.
source: For example, if the task is to detect weak (low amplitude) inputs, performance would be higher if top down modulations (such as attention) reduced the level of noise, and thus increased the degree of population synchrony (Figure 9b) without significantly changing firing rates.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model, shown in Figure 9b.

claim: Higher detection performance could correlate with a stronger level of Gamma oscillations.
source: We can thus expect higher detection performance to correlate with a stronger level of Gamma oscillations (Figure 9c).
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model, shown in Figure 9c.

claim: This could account for certain attention-dependent increases in gamma-power and its correlation with behavioural performance.
source: This could account for certain attention-dependent increases in gamma-power and its correlation with behavioural performance (see Discussion).
evidence: This is stated as a potential explanation for empirical observations.

claim: A similar correlation between behavioural performance and Gamma power could arise from purely bottom up effects, where trial-by-trial changes in input strength result in more detection and more Gamma oscillations.
source: Note that a similar correlation between behavioural performance and Gamma power could arise from purely bottom up effects. In the presence of input noise causing trial-by-trial changes in input strength, trials with stronger input amplitude would result in more detection but also exhibit more Gamma oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as an alternative explanation.

claim: In the bottom-up scenario, the increase in Gamma power would be associated with a commensurate increase in population firing rate.
source: In that case, however, the increase in Gamma power would be associated with a commensurate increase in population firing rate.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of the bottom-up explanation.

claim: With readout weights held constant, neural firing rates in the model are inversely proportional to the network size.
source: With readout weights held constant, neural firing rates in our model are inversely proportional to the network size (such that the population firing rate stays constant; Figure 10a).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 10a.

claim: The optimal coding performance was practically unaltered by increasing or decreasing the population size by a factor of two.
source: The optimal coding performance was practically unaltered by increasing or decreasing the population size by a factor of two, although there was a small trend for the optimal noise magnitude to increase with population size (Figure 10b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 10b.

claim: The oscillatory dynamics were unaltered by varying the network size.
source: The oscillatory dynamics were unaltered by varying the network size (Figure 10c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 10c.

claim: Varying the number of inhibitory neurons (while keeping the number of excitatory neurons constant) had little effect on coding performance or oscillatory dynamics.
source: Varying the number of inhibitory neurons (while keeping the number of excitatory neurons constant), had a similar effect on inhibitory firing rates (Figure 10d), with little effect on coding performance or oscillatory dynamics (Figure 10e–f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 10d, 10e, and 10f.

claim: Increasing the synaptic delay meant that more neurons fired on each oscillation cycle before receiving recurrent inhibition, and thus resulted in decreased coding performance.
source: Increasing the synaptic delay meant that more neurons fired on each oscillation cycle before receiving recurrent inhibition, and thus resulted in decreased coding performance (Figure 11 b), and larger, lower frequency oscillations (Figure 11c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 11b and 11c.

claim: Increasing the synaptic delay resulted in larger, lower frequency oscillations.
source: Increasing the synaptic delay meant that more neurons fired on each oscillation cycle before receiving recurrent inhibition, and thus resulted in decreased coding performance (Figure 11 b), and larger, lower frequency oscillations (Figure 11c).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 11c.

claim: The results provide a functional explanation for why cortical networks operate in a regime in which global oscillations in population firing rates occur alongside individual neurons with low, irregular, firing rates.
source: Our results provide a functional explanation for why cortical networks operate in a regime in which: (i) global oscillations in population firing rates occur alongside individual neurons with low, irregular, firing rates (Brunel and Hakim, 1999) (ii) there is a tight balance between excitation and inhibition (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Cafaro and Rieke, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the paper with supporting citations.

claim: The results provide a functional explanation for why there is a tight balance between excitation and inhibition in cortical networks.
source: Our results provide a functional explanation for why cortical networks operate in a regime in which: (i) global oscillations in population firing rates occur alongside individual neurons with low, irregular, firing rates (Brunel and Hakim, 1999) (ii) there is a tight balance between excitation and inhibition (Atallah and Scanziani, 2009; Wehr and Zador, 2003; Cafaro and Rieke, 2010).
evidence: This is stated as a main conclusion of the paper with supporting citations.

claim: Brunel & colleagues derived the conditions under which a recurrent network of integrate-and-fire neurons with sparse irregular firing rates exhibits fast global oscillations.
source: Previously, Brunel & colleagues derived the conditions under which a recurrent network of integrate-and-fire neurons with sparse irregular firing rates exhibits fast global oscillations (Brunel and Hakim, 1999; Renart et al., 2010; Brunel and Wang, 2003; Mazzoni et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as prior work with supporting citations.

claim: Previous balanced network models assume sparse connections (and/or weak connectivity), in which the probability of connections (and/or connection strengths) scales inversely with the number of neurons.
source: For example, they assume sparse connections (and/or weak connectivity), in which the probability of connections (and/or connection strengths) scales inversely with the number of neurons.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of previous models.

claim: The connections in the current model are non-sparse and finite.
source: In contrast, the connections in our network are non-sparse and finite.
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of the current model.

claim: Previous models of balanced neural networks typically consider medium to large neural populations, for which finite size effects are limited.
source: Previous models of balanced neural networks typically consider medium to large neural populations, for which finite size effects are limited.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of previous models.

claim: The recurrent network proposed here is particularly relevant to networks with a relatively small number of neurons (i.e. hundreds, rather than thousands, of neurons per input dimension).
source: In contrast, the recurrent network proposed here is particularly relevant to networks with a relatively small number of neurons (i.e. hundreds, rather than thousands, of neurons per input dimension).
evidence: This is stated as a distinguishing feature of the current model.

claim: In cases where a very large number of neurons encode a low-dimensional input, fluctuations in firing rate due to Poisson noise can be averaged out, and thus are not a limiting factor for coding accuracy.
source: This is because in cases where a very large number of neurons encode a low-dimensional input, fluctuations in firing rate due to Poisson noise can be averaged out, and thus are not a limiting factor for coding accuracy.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why the model is most relevant to smaller networks.

claim: The most important distinction between the current work and previous mean-field models lies in the way the network is constructed.
source: The most important distinction between our work and previous mean-field models lies in the way the network is constructed.
evidence: This is stated as a key difference from prior work.

claim: In the current work, the network connectivity and dynamics are derived from functional principles, in order to minimise a specific loss function.
source: In our work, the network connectivity and dynamics are derived from functional principles, in order to minimise a specific loss function (i.e. the squared difference between the neural reconstruction and input signal).
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the modeling approach.

claim: Balanced inhibition and excitation are not imposed in the current model, but rather, required for efficient coding.
source: For example, balanced inhibition and excitation are not imposed in our model, but rather, required for efficient coding.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding of the model.

claim: While previous models showed mechanistically how fast oscillations can emerge in a network with slow irregular firing rates, the current work shows that these dynamics are in fact required for optimal efficient coding.
source: Further, while previous models showed mechanistically how fast oscillations can emerge in a network with slow irregular firing rates (Brunel and Hakim, 1999), our work goes further, showing that these dynamics are in fact required for optimal efficient coding.
evidence: This is stated as a key contribution of the current work with a supporting citation.

claim: While efficient coding in a recurrent network leads to global oscillations, the reverse is not true: just because a network oscillates, does not mean that it is performing efficiently.
source: Finally, it is important to realise that, while efficient coding in a recurrent network leads to global oscillations, the reverse is not true: just because a network oscillates, does not mean that it is performing efficiently.
evidence: This is stated as an important caveat.

claim: When recurrent connection strengths are randomised, the coding performance of the network is greatly reduced, despite the fact that the network dynamics and firing rate power spectrum are virtually unchanged.
source: In contrast, when we randomised the recurrent connection strengths (Figure 12c–d; see Materials and methods), the coding performance of the network was greatly reduced (Figure 12e), despite the fact that the network dynamics and firing rate power spectrum were virtually unchanged (Figure 12f).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figures 12c-f.

claim: The coherence between excitatory and inhibitory current oscillations (i.e. the level of balance) is a much more reliable signature of efficient coding than global population synchrony.
source: Indeed, the coherence between excitatory and inhibitory current oscillations (i.e. the level of balance) is a much more reliable signature of efficient coding than global population synchrony.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the randomized connection analysis.

claim: Only networks with an intracellular detailed balance between excitatory and inhibitory currents achieve high coding performance.
source: While population synchrony can occur in globally balanced network as well, only networks with an intracellular detailed balance between excitatory and inhibitory currents achieve high coding performance.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding.

claim: Previous work on efficient coding has mostly concentrated on using information theory to ask what information 'should' be represented by sensory systems.
source: Previous work on efficient coding has mostly concentrated on using information theory to ask what information 'should' be represented by sensory systems (Simoncelli and Olshausen, 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of prior work with a supporting citation.

claim: Researchers have begun to ask, mechanistically, how neural networks should be setup in order to operate as efficiently as possible.
source: Recently, however, researchers have begun to ask, mechanistically, how neural networks should be setup in order to operate as efficiently as possible (Boerlin et al., 2013; Boerlin and Denève, 2011; Deneve, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a recent trend in the field with supporting citations.

claim: According to information theory, in the low-noise limit, the most efficient spiking representation will be one in which the spike trains of different neurons are statistically independent, and thus, there are no oscillations.
source: For example, according to information theory, in the low-noise limit, the most efficient spiking representation will be one in which the spike trains of different neurons are statistically independent, and thus, there are no oscillations.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from information theory.

claim: Considering biological constraints such as synaptic delays changes the conclusions about efficient coding, with oscillations emerging even in a regime with low input-noise.
source: Considering these constraints changes our conclusions. Specifically, contrary to what one might expect from a purely information theoretical analysis, we find that oscillations emerge (even in a regime with low input-noise) as a consequence of neurons performing as efficiently as possible given synaptic delays, and should not be removed at all cost.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding that differs from information-theoretic predictions.

claim: Deneve, Machens and colleagues described how a population of spiking neurons can efficiently encode a dynamic input variable.
source: Previously, Deneve, Machens and colleagues described how a population of spiking neurons can efficiently encode a dynamic input variable (Boerlin et al., 2013; Boerlin and Denève, 2011; Deneve, 2008; Bourdoukan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as prior work with supporting citations.

claim: A recurrent population of integrate-and-fire neurons with dynamics and connectivity tuned for efficient coding maintains a balance between excitation and inhibition, exhibits Poisson-like spike statistics, and is highly robust against perturbations such as neuronal cell death.
source: In this work, we showed that a recurrent population of integrate-and-fire neurons with dynamics and connectivity tuned for efficient coding maintains a balance between excitation and inhibition, exhibits Poisson-like spike statistics (Boerlin et al., 2013), and is highly robust against perturbations such as neuronal cell death.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of prior work with a supporting citation.

claim: Previous work did not demonstrate a relation between efficient coding and neural oscillations because it considered an idealised network with instantaneous synapses.
source: However, we did not previously demonstrate a relation between efficient coding and neural oscillations. The main reason for this is that we always considered an idealised network, with instantaneous synapses.
evidence: This is stated as an explanation for why oscillations were not observed in prior work.

claim: In the idealised network with instantaneous synapses, only one cell fires at a time, and oscillations are generally extremely weak and fast.
source: In this idealised network, only one cell fires at a time. As a result, oscillations are generally extremely weak and fast (with frequency equal to the population firing rate), and thus, completely washed out in a large network with added noise and/or heterogenous read-out weights.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the idealized model.

claim: In a network with finite synaptic delays, more than one neuron may fire per oscillation cycle, before the arrival of inhibition, resulting in much stronger oscillations.
source: In contrast, in a network with finite synaptic delays, more than one neuron may fire per oscillation cycle, before the arrival of inhibition. As a result, oscillations are generally much stronger, even with significant added noise and/or heterogenous read-out weights.
evidence: This is stated as a key difference between the idealized and realistic models.

claim: Directing attention to a particular stimulus feature/location has been shown to increase the gamma-band synchronisation of visual neurons that respond to the attended feature/location.
source: Directing attention to a particular stimulus feature/location has been shown to increase the gamma-band synchronisation of visual neurons that respond to the attended feature/location (Fries et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with a supporting citation.

claim: Attentional modulations that increase the strength of gamma-band oscillations will serve to increase perceptual discrimination of low contrast stimuli.
source: Here, we show that attentional modulations that increase the strength of gamma-band oscillations will serve to increase perceptual discrimination of low contrast stimuli.
evidence: This is stated as a prediction from the model shown in Figure 9.

claim: Attentional modulation could be achieved by decreasing noise fluctuations, or modulating the effective gain of feed-forward or recurrent connections.
source: Such attentional modulation could be achieved in a number of different ways, for example, by decreasing noise fluctuations, or modulating the effective gain of feed-forward or recurrent connections (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Mitchell et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation about mechanisms with supporting citations.

claim: Various sources of noise (e.g. such as synaptic failure), often thought of as a 'problem' for neural coding, may in fact help neural networks achieve higher coding performance than would otherwise be possible.
source: An interesting aspect of our work is that it suggests various sources of noise (e.g. such as synaptic failure), often thought of as a 'problem' for neural coding, may in fact help neural networks achieve higher coding performance than would otherwise be possible.
evidence: This is stated as a key insight from the work.

claim: With the right level of noise, fewer neurons fired on each oscillation cycle, resulting in increased coding performance.
source: With the right level of noise, fewer neurons fired on each oscillation cycle, resulting in increased coding performance.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the model.

claim: The phenomena where noise fluctuations increase the signal processing performance of a system is often referred to as 'stochastic resonance'.
source: This phenomena, where noise fluctuations increase the signal processing performance of a system, is often referred to as 'stochastic resonance' (Benzi et al., 1981; Faisal et al., 2008), and has been observed in multiple sensory systems, including cat visual neurons (Longtin et al., 1991; Levin and Miller, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a connection to an established phenomenon with supporting citations.

claim: Stochastic resonance has been observed in multiple sensory systems, including cat visual neurons.
source: This phenomena, where noise fluctuations increase the signal processing performance of a system, is often referred to as 'stochastic resonance' (Benzi et al., 1981; Faisal et al., 2008), and has been observed in multiple sensory systems, including cat visual neurons (Longtin et al., 1991; Levin and Miller, 1996).
evidence: This is stated as an empirical observation with supporting citations.

claim: Previously, stochastic resonance has usually been seen as a method to amplify sub-threshold sensory signals that would not normally drive neurons to spike.
source: Previously however, stochastic resonance has usually been seen as a method to amplify sub-threshold sensory signals that would not normally drive neurons to spike.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of prior understanding.

claim: In the current work, noise desynchronises neurons that receive similar recurrent inputs, increasing the coding efficiency of the population.
source: Here, in contrast, noise desynchronises neurons that receive similar recurrent inputs, increasing the coding efficiency of the population.
evidence: This is stated as a novel mechanism for stochastic resonance.

claim: Neurons in the model have voltage-driven synapses, while real synapses are better approximated by conductance based models.
source: For example, neurons in our model have voltage-driven synapses, while real synapses are better approximated by conductance based models.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: The slow time constant (100 ms) required in the simulations to achieve high coding performance contrasts with the relatively fast (∼10–20 ms) membrane time constants observed experimentally.
source: Further, the slow time constant (100 ms), required in our simulations to achieve high coding performance, contrasts with the relatively fast (∼10–20 ms) membrane time constants observed experimentally.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model.

claim: Neural oscillations have been hypothesised to fulfill a number of different functional roles, including feature binding, gating communication between different neural assemblies, encoding feed-forward and feed-back prediction errors, and facilitating 'phase codes'.
source: Neural oscillations have been hypothesised to fulfill a number of different functional roles, including feature binding (Singer, 1999), gating communication between different neural assemblies (Fries, 2005; Womelsdorf et al., 2007; Akam and Kullmann, 2010), encoding feed-forward and feed-back prediction errors (Arnal et al., 2011; Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Bastos et al., 2012) and facilitating 'phase codes' in which information is communicated via the timing of spikes relative to the ongoing oscillation cycle (Buzsáki and Chrobak, 1995).
evidence: This is stated as a summary of alternative theories with supporting citations.

claim: Many theories propose new ways in which oscillations encode incoming sensory information.
source: Many of these theories propose new ways in which oscillations encode incoming sensory information.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of alternative theories.

claim: In the current work, network oscillations do not directly code for anything, but rather, are predicted as a consequence of efficient rate coding.
source: In contrast, in our work network oscillations do not directly code for anything, but rather, are predicted as a consequence of efficient rate coding, an idea whose origins go back more than 50 years (Barlow, 1961).
evidence: This is stated as a key distinction from alternative theories with a supporting citation.
